name: Media device kinds and counts
plain: Counts of cameras, microphones and speakers, without names, before any permission.
meaning: Tells a site whether the device has a camera and mic and how many outputs. Without permission labels and device IDs are empty, but kinds and counts leak a hardware profile (laptop vs headset vs desktop).

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can count your cameras, mics, and speakers without names before you allow access
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page checks for a camera or mic
can: See whether you have a camera or microphone
Guess a laptop, headset, or desktop setup from the counts
See full device names after you allow camera or mic
cannot: See device names or IDs before you allow camera or mic
Turn on your camera or microphone
See which device is in use
limits.reach_label: Counts only, until you allow it

story.what_it_is: Tells a page how many cameras, microphones and speakers you have, without names, before you give permission.

marketing.name: MediaDevices.enumerateDevices
marketing.pitch: Docs explain it as a way to list device kinds, with names hidden until permission is given.

story.for_you: You never see it. Before you allow anything, a video call page can still tell that you have one camera and two microphones, so it can show the right buttons. It cannot see your name labels yet.
story.for_makers: Video call and recording sites need to know whether to offer camera and microphone options. The counts also say something about your setup, such as a headset or a studio mic. Fingerprinters use it for that reason.

use_cases.example: A video call page shows a camera button only when it sees a camera, before the permission pop-up.
A browser party game with voice chat shows a mic option only for devices that have one.
An online class platform checks you have a camera and mic before a live lesson starts.
A web streaming studio shows a list of inputs after you press start and offers extras if you have two cameras.
A telehealth visit checks that you can be seen and heard before the doctor joins.
A fraud tool sees a device with no audio outputs and treats it as a server or bot.
An IT help page tests meeting room devices from the browser before a big call.

technical_bounds: No labels or hardware IDs until permission

linkedin.how: Media devices (cameras, mics, speakers) enumerated. Read by the LinkedIn APFC fingerprint script (48 features, alleged by BrowserGate, partly confirmed by BleepingComputer).

history.change: Labels blank without permission; deviceId per-origin partitioned
